stem: Under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, when must the employer make the hepatitis B vaccination series available to a newly hired technologist with occupational exposure?
choices: Only after the technologist reports a needlestick or other exposure incident
Within 90 days of hire, with the cost shared by the employee
After required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment, at no cost
Only if a prescreening antibody test shows the technologist is not immune
explanation: OSHA requires the vaccine to be made available after training and within 10 working days of initial assignment, at no cost to the employee. Waiting for an exposure incident misses the pre-exposure requirement, and prescreening may not be made a prerequisite for vaccination.

stem: Which body fluid is classified as other potentially infectious material (OPIM) under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard even when no blood is visible?
choices: Cerebrospinal fluid
Urine without visible blood
Nasal secretions without visible blood
Sweat
explanation: OSHA lists cerebrospinal fluid with synovial, pleural, pericardial, peritoneal and amniotic fluids, semen and vaginal secretions as OPIM. Urine, tears and sweat become OPIM only when visibly contaminated with blood or when body fluids cannot be differentiated.

stem: A new refrigerator will be used to store patient serum and plasma specimens. How must it be labeled under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard?
choices: A yellow caution label reading "Specimens only"
A fluorescent orange or orange-red biohazard label
A GHS health-hazard pictogram with the signal word "Warning"
No label; only shipping containers need one
explanation: OSHA requires warning labels on refrigerators and freezers containing blood or OPIM, and the labels must be fluorescent orange or orange-red with the biohazard legend in a contrasting color. GHS pictograms communicate chemical hazards, not biohazards.

stem: For how long must an employer keep the medical record of a technologist with occupational exposure under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard?
choices: 3 years from the date the record was created
Until the hepatitis B vaccination series is completed
5 years after the employee leaves the job
At least the duration of employment plus 30 years
explanation: Bloodborne pathogens medical records must be kept for at least the duration of employment plus 30 years. The 3-year period applies to training records, not medical records.

stem: While pipetting patient serum, a technologist notices a small tear in one glove. What should be done?
choices: Finish the current run first, then change both gloves
Remove the gloves, wash hands, and put on new gloves
Cover the tear with tape and keep working
Wipe the glove with 70% alcohol and keep working
explanation: Disposable gloves must be replaced as soon as feasible when torn, and hands are washed after glove removal. Disposable gloves may not be washed or decontaminated for reuse, so wiping or taping the glove is not acceptable.

stem: Which activity is prohibited at a laboratory bench where blood specimens are processed?
choices: Applying lip balm
Wearing a fluid-resistant laboratory coat
Using a mechanical pipetting device
Recording results on a paper worksheet
explanation: OSHA prohibits eating, drinking, smoking, applying cosmetics or lip balm and handling contact lenses where occupational exposure is reasonably likely. Mechanical pipetting is the required alternative to mouth pipetting, which is prohibited.

stem: A technologist wearing a fluid-resistant lab coat in specimen processing is leaving for a break in the cafeteria. What should be done with the lab coat?
choices: Wear it on break if it has no visible blood
Take it home to wash with personal laundry
Turn it inside out and wear it on break
Remove it before leaving the work area
explanation: All PPE must be removed before leaving the work area and placed in a designated area or container. The employer, not the employee, cleans and launders PPE, so taking it home is not acceptable.

stem: According to the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, when must hands be washed after removing gloves worn to handle blood specimens?
choices: Only if the gloves were torn or punctured
Only at the end of the shift
Immediately or as soon as feasible after glove removal
Only if blood is visible on the hands
explanation: OSHA requires hand washing immediately or as soon as feasible after removing gloves or other PPE. Gloves can have unnoticed defects, so washing only after a visible tear is not sufficient.

stem: Laboratory culture work with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which is transmitted by the respiratory route, is typically performed at which biosafety level?
choices: BSL-1
BSL-2
BSL-3
BSL-4
explanation: BSL-3 is used for indigenous or exotic microbes that can cause serious or lethal disease through respiratory transmission, such as M. tuberculosis. BSL-4 is reserved for dangerous exotic agents such as Ebola and Marburg viruses.

stem: Which biological safety cabinet is used most often in clinical laboratories because it protects both the worker and the specimen or culture being handled?
choices: Class I
Class II
Class III
Chemical fume hood
explanation: Class II cabinets, with HEPA-filtered vertical airflow, protect personnel and the product and are the type used most often in clinical laboratories. A Class I cabinet protects the worker and environment but not the product, and a fume hood is not a biological safety cabinet.

stem: A technologist working in a Class II biological safety cabinet wants to flame an inoculating loop. What is the best practice?
choices: Place a Bunsen burner just inside the front grille
Switch off the cabinet blower briefly while flaming
Close the sash completely while flaming
Use a sterile disposable loop instead of a flame
explanation: Open flames should not be used inside a BSC because they disrupt the protective airflow and create a fire hazard. Turning off the blower or blocking the front grille also destroys containment.

stem: In a BSL-2 clinical microbiology laboratory, which task should be performed inside a biological safety cabinet?
choices: Grinding a tissue specimen for culture
Examining a stained smear under the microscope
Entering culture results into the laboratory information system
Labeling empty culture plates before inoculation
explanation: At BSL-2, procedures that can cause infection through aerosols or splashes, such as tissue grinding, are performed in a biological safety cabinet. Reading a fixed, stained smear or doing clerical tasks does not generate infectious aerosols.

stem: On a chemical label required by the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard, what does the signal word "Danger" indicate compared with "Warning"?
choices: A more severe hazard
A less severe hazard
A hazard that applies only during shipping
A chemical that has no physical hazards
explanation: OSHA uses two signal words: "Danger" for more severe hazards and "Warning" for less severe hazards. The signal word appears on shipped-container labels with the pictograms and hazard statements.

stem: A technologist needs to know which gloves and eye protection to wear with a new fixative. Which section of the 16-section safety data sheet (SDS) should be checked?
choices: Section 2, Hazard(s) identification
Section 4, First-aid measures
Section 8, Exposure controls/personal protection
Section 11, Toxicological information
explanation: Section 8 of the SDS gives exposure controls and personal protective equipment. Section 4 covers first aid after an exposure, not the PPE needed to prevent one.

stem: Methanol is poured from a labeled stock bottle into a squeeze bottle that will stay on the staining bench for all staff to use over several shifts. What does the OSHA Hazard Communication Standard require?
choices: No label, because portable containers are always exempt
Label the squeeze bottle with the product identifier and hazard information
A label showing only the date of transfer
A label only if the bottle holds more than 1 liter
explanation: The portable-container exemption applies only when the chemical is for immediate use by the person who transferred it within the same work shift. A shared container kept across shifts is a workplace container and needs the product identifier and hazard information.

stem: Which OSHA standard requires a laboratory to have a written Chemical Hygiene Plan and a designated Chemical Hygiene Officer?
choices: 29 CFR 1910.1030, the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard
29 CFR 1910.1200, the Hazard Communication Standard
29 CFR 1910.157, Portable fire extinguishers
29 CFR 1910.1450, the Laboratory Standard
explanation: The OSHA Laboratory Standard (29 CFR 1910.1450) requires a written Chemical Hygiene Plan, a Chemical Hygiene Officer, and at least annual review of the plan. The Hazard Communication Standard covers labels, SDSs and training but does not require a Chemical Hygiene Plan.

stem: A fire starts in the wiring of an energized analyzer. Which extinguisher class is designed for this type of fire?
choices: Class A
Class B
Class C
Class D
explanation: Fires in wiring and energized electrical equipment require an extinguisher labeled C. Class A is for ordinary combustibles such as paper and wood, and Class D is for combustible metals.

stem: Using the PASS technique on a small fire, where should the extinguisher nozzle be aimed?
choices: At the top of the flames
Low, at the base of the fire
At the smoke above the fire
At the wall behind the fire
explanation: PASS means pull the pin, aim low at the base of the fire, squeeze the handle, and sweep side to side. Aiming at the flames or smoke does not reach the burning fuel.

stem: Before starting a centrifuge, a technologist sees that its power cord insulation is cracked and frayed. What should be done?
choices: Wrap the damaged area with electrical tape and run it
Run today's specimens and report the cord at shift end
Plug it into an extension cord to reduce strain on the cord
Remove the centrifuge from service and report it for repair
explanation: OSHA requires cord-and-plug equipment to be inspected before use, and damaged items must be removed from service until repaired and tested. Using it with a temporary tape repair still exposes workers to shock and fire hazards.

stem: A small fire involves spilled ethanol on a laboratory bench. Which portable extinguisher is appropriate?
choices: Carbon dioxide extinguisher rated for Class B and C fires
Air-pressurized water extinguisher rated for Class A fires
Dry powder extinguisher rated only for Class D metal fires
No extinguisher; blow out the flames with compressed air
explanation: Flammable liquid fires are Class B, and CO2 extinguishers are designed for Class B and C fires. Water should never be used on flammable liquid fires because it is ineffective and can spread the burning liquid.

stem: Patient specimens that may contain pathogens but do not meet the high-risk Category A criteria are shipped under which UN number and proper shipping name?
choices: UN 2814, Infectious Substance, Affecting Humans
UN 3373, Biological Substance, Category B
UN 2900, Infectious Substance, Affecting Animals only
UN 1845, Carbon dioxide, solid (dry ice)
explanation: Low- and moderate-risk specimens are packaged, labeled and shipped as Category B infectious substances (UN 3373). UN 2814 is used for high-risk Category A infectious substances affecting humans.

stem: When triple-packaging a liquid serum specimen for shipment, where is the absorbent material placed?
choices: Between the primary receptacle and the secondary receptacle
Between the secondary receptacle and the outer packaging
Inside the primary tube with the specimen
Outside the outer box, under the shipping label
explanation: For liquid specimens, absorbent material goes between the leakproof primary receptacle and the leakproof secondary receptacle so it can contain a leak. The space between the secondary receptacle and outer packaging holds the list of contents and paperwork.

stem: Where should the itemized list of contents and specimen paperwork be placed in a UN 3373 triple package?
choices: Inside the secondary receptacle with the specimen tubes
Taped directly to the primary receptacle
Mailed separately after the package is delivered
Between the secondary receptacle and the outer packaging
explanation: The list of contents and paperwork go between the secondary receptacle and the outer packaging, where they stay dry and can be read without opening the leakproof layers. Placing paperwork inside the secondary receptacle risks contaminating it if a tube leaks.

stem: A technologist sustains a needlestick from a needle used on a patient. What should be done first?
choices: Finish processing the specimens, then report
Wait for the source patient's HIV result before acting
Wash the puncture site with soap and water
Cover the site with a bandage and keep working
explanation: CDC first aid is to wash the needlestick site with soap and water, then report to the supervisor and seek medical care immediately. Delaying care or reporting can delay post-exposure prophylaxis.

stem: Formalin splashes into a technologist's eye. How long should the eye be flushed at the eyewash station?
choices: At least 15 minutes
30 seconds
2 minutes
Until the stinging stops
explanation: Chemical splashes to the eye should be flushed with running water or saline for at least 15 minutes, followed by prompt medical care. Shorter flushing, or stopping when pain eases, can leave chemical in the eye.

stem: After an occupational exposure to blood from a patient with HIV, when must HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) be started to be effective?
choices: Within 7 days of the exposure
As soon as possible, and within 72 hours
Only after the employee's baseline HIV test is positive
Within 30 days of the exposure
explanation: CDC states PEP must be started within 72 hours of exposure, and the sooner it starts the better. A positive baseline test would mean prior infection, which PEP cannot prevent.

stem: A flask of broth culture of a pathogenic organism breaks and spills across a microbiology bench. Which approach follows CDC recommendations?
choices: Wipe up the liquid with paper towels, then rinse the bench with tap water
Spray with water to dilute the culture, then mop up
Confine it, flood it with liquid germicide, then clean and decontaminate
Let the culture dry before sweeping up the glass
explanation: For large spills of concentrated infectious agents, CDC recommends confining the area, flooding it with a liquid chemical germicide before cleaning, and decontaminating with fresh germicide of at least intermediate-level potency. Wiping or rinsing without a germicide spreads viable organisms.

stem: Which waste container is intended for used glass slides and tubes with small amounts of blood?
choices: Puncture-resistant sharps container
Red biohazard bag
Regular trash container
Glass recycling bin
explanation: Puncture-resistant containers at the point of use hold discarded slides or tubes with small amounts of blood, needles, scalpel blades and other sharps. A biohazard bag can be punctured by glass, exposing handlers.

stem: How should used microbiology culture plates and stocks of microorganisms be handled before final disposal?
choices: Discard them in regular trash once the lids are taped
Pour bleach over them and flush them down the sink
Freeze them until the waste hauler arrives
Decontaminate them on site, such as by autoclaving
explanation: CDC recommends on-site decontamination of microbiology cultures and stocks, preferably within the laboratory, historically by autoclaving (steam sterilization) or incineration. Taping lids does not inactivate the high concentration of organisms.

stem: Under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, which item is regulated waste?
choices: Gloves with no visible blood that were worn to handle capped tubes
Gauze caked with dried blood that could flake off during handling
An empty cardboard reagent box
A paper towel used after hand washing
explanation: Regulated waste includes items caked with dried blood or OPIM that can release these materials during handling, as well as liquid or semi-liquid blood and contaminated sharps. Gloves with no visible blood would not release blood if compressed, so they are not regulated waste under this definition.

stem: Which federal agency certifies and regulates clinical laboratories for the quality of patient testing?
choices: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), through CLIA
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
explanation: CMS regulates laboratory testing performed on humans in the United States through the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA), with requirements that scale to the complexity of the test method. OSHA is the tempting answer because it writes the safety rules the bench works under, but it governs worker protection, not the quality of patient results; CDC and FDA are CLIA partners without the certifying role.

stem: Which testing falls under CLIA?
choices: Only testing performed in hospital laboratories
Only testing billed to Medicare or Medicaid
Any testing of materials from the human body for health assessment, diagnosis, prevention, or treatment
Only moderate- and high-complexity testing
explanation: CLIA covers testing of human specimens for the purpose of assessing health or diagnosing, preventing, or treating disease, wherever that testing is performed. Limiting it to hospitals is the common misread: physician office laboratories and clinics are covered too. The narrow exceptions are SAMHSA-regulated drug testing, forensic testing, and research that does not report patient-specific results.

stem: A clinic holding a Certificate of Waiver installs a moderate-complexity chemistry analyzer. What must it do before running patient samples on it?
choices: Apply for the certificate type that matches the highest complexity of testing it performs
Nothing: every CLIA certificate permits waived testing, so the new analyzer is covered
Report the new instrument at the next biennial certificate renewal
Have a reference laboratory confirm the first month of results
explanation: A laboratory applies for the certificate matching the highest complexity of testing it performs, so moderate-complexity work needs a nonwaived certificate before patient samples are run. It is true that every certificate type allows waived testing, which makes that option tempting, but it is a floor, not a ceiling: a Certificate of Waiver covers waived tests only.

stem: How long is a CLIA certificate effective before it must be renewed?
choices: One year
Two years
Three years
Indefinitely, as long as the annual fee is paid
explanation: Every type of CLIA certificate is effective for two years, after which the laboratory renews it. The indefinite option is tempting because fees are a familiar part of the programme, but no CLIA certificate runs without a renewal cycle.

stem: Which body assigns a test system its complexity category, and what are the CLIA groupings?
choices: CMS assigns it; the groupings are simple and complex
CDC assigns it; the groupings are screening and confirmatory
The accrediting organization assigns it; the groupings are routine and esoteric
FDA assigns it; tests are waived or nonwaived, with nonwaived covering moderate and high complexity
explanation: FDA categorizes test systems as waived (simple, with a low risk of an incorrect result) or nonwaived, and nonwaived covers both moderate and high complexity. CMS is the tempting answer because CMS issues the certificates and enforces CLIA, but it is the FDA categorization that decides which certificate a laboratory needs.

stem: A laboratory wants to bring up a test system that FDA has not yet categorized for complexity. How is it treated?
choices: As high complexity, until it is categorized
As moderate complexity, until it is categorized
It may not be used for patient testing in any CLIA laboratory
It takes the category of the most similar test system already on the market
explanation: A test system that has not been categorized defaults to high complexity. FDA scores seven criteria from 1 to 3; a total score of 12 or less makes the test moderate complexity and a score above 12 makes it high complexity. Moderate is tempting because it sits in the middle, but until a categorization exists the conservative assumption — the highest personnel and quality requirements — is what applies.

stem: What does CLIA require of the laboratory director at a site holding a Certificate of Waiver?
choices: A doctoral-level director is required, as in every CLIA laboratory
The site must name a laboratory director, but no federal education or experience qualifications apply to that role under a Certificate of Waiver
No laboratory director is needed; the practice manager signs the application
The director must be board certified in clinical pathology
explanation: A Certificate of Waiver laboratory must have a laboratory director, but CLIA sets no federal education or experience requirements for that position. The doctoral-level answer is tempting because directors of nonwaived laboratories do have to meet CLIA education, training, and experience requirements — the complexity of the testing is what draws the line.

stem: A physician office laboratory applies for a certificate covering provider-performed microscopy and other moderate-complexity testing. What applies to its director?
choices: Any licensed physician qualifies, regardless of laboratory training
A director is optional as long as a consultant reviews results monthly
The director must meet CLIA's education, training, and experience requirements, and documentation goes in with the application
The state survey agency appoints the director
explanation: Directors of laboratories performing nonwaived testing — moderate complexity, high complexity, or provider-performed microscopy — must meet CLIA's education, training, and experience requirements, and the laboratory submits proof of those qualifications with its application. A medical licence alone is the tempting answer, but licensure is not the same as the director qualifications CLIA specifies.

stem: Proficiency testing samples arrive and a supervisor suggests the most experienced technologist run all of them so the laboratory scores well. Why is that wrong?
choices: PT samples must be tested like patient specimens, by the staff who routinely perform that testing, because PT validates the testing process and the competency of testing personnel
Only the laboratory director may handle PT samples
PT samples must be split and run by every employee in the department
It is acceptable, because PT scores belong to the laboratory rather than to individuals
explanation: PT exists to validate the accuracy and reliability of the laboratory's testing process, including the competency of the personnel who perform it, so the samples are handled in the routine way by the routine staff. Funnelling every sample to the strongest technologist produces a score that says nothing about the testing patients actually receive.

stem: Among the federal partners in the CLIA programme, which one monitors proficiency testing practices and develops technical standards and laboratory practice guidelines, including those for cytology?
choices: CMS
FDA
CDC
The state survey agency
explanation: CDC's CLIA role is the technical one: monitoring proficiency testing practices and developing technical standards and laboratory practice guidelines, including cytology guidelines. CMS is tempting because it issues certificates and enforces the regulations, and FDA categorizes test complexity; the three agencies share the programme.

stem: Which laboratories must enrol in an approved proficiency testing programme?
choices: Every CLIA laboratory, including sites that perform only waived tests
Only laboratories holding a Certificate of Accreditation
Only hospital laboratories
Those performing nonwaived testing for regulated analytes
explanation: CLIA-certificated laboratories that perform nonwaived testing for regulated analytes must enrol in an approved PT programme. Sweeping in waived-only sites is the tempting overreach: the PT requirement follows the complexity of the testing, not the mere fact of holding a certificate.

stem: A proficiency testing result looks implausible, and a colleague offers to send the remaining PT material to the reference laboratory for confirmation before it is reported. What do you do?
choices: Refuse: PT samples may not be referred to another laboratory; report the result this laboratory obtained
Agree, because confirming an odd result before reporting is good practice
Agree, and report the reference laboratory's result instead
Discard the sample and request a replacement shipment
explanation: PT samples are treated exactly like patient specimens with one addition: they may not be referred to another laboratory for testing. Confirming a strange result sounds like diligence, which is what makes it the trap — PT referral is a violation that puts the laboratory's CLIA certificate at risk. Report what this laboratory's own method produced, then investigate the method.

stem: How must a proficiency testing sample be analysed?
choices: In duplicate on both analyzers, reporting the pair that agrees best
On the same instrument and method, in the same manner, and the same number of times as a patient specimen
By whichever method the PT provider recommends, even if the laboratory uses another
Three times, reporting the mean of the three results
explanation: A PT sample is run with the laboratory's routine method, in the same manner and the same number of times as a patient specimen, which is what makes the score a statement about routine patient testing. Extra replicates and picking the best agreement is special handling, and special handling defeats the purpose of the exercise.

stem: Which enrolment does CLIA require for gynecologic cytology proficiency testing?
choices: The laboratory only
The laboratory and each individual who examines gynecologic cytology slides, in an approved programme such as those run by CAP or ASCP
The cytotechnologists only; pathologists are exempt
Enrolment is recommended rather than required
explanation: Gyn cytology PT is required both for the laboratory and for every individual who examines gyn cytology slides, through an approved programme — CAP and ASCP operate them. Laboratory-level enrolment alone is the familiar pattern from chemistry and haematology PT, which is exactly why it is the tempting answer here.

stem: What does CLIA require of a nonwaived laboratory to assure the quality of its results?
choices: Quality control run only when a clinician questions a result
Quality control run on the days inspectors are on site
Documented quality control and quality assurance measures covering the complete testing process, so results are accurate and precise
Review of every abnormal result by a second technologist
explanation: CLIA requires quality control and quality assurance measures across the complete testing process so that results are accurate and precise. Running QC only in response to a complaint or an inspection inverts the purpose: QC is what catches the error before the result leaves the laboratory.

stem: A research study tests patient specimens but never reports results for patient care. The team now wants to release one result to the patient's physician. What changes?
choices: Nothing: research testing is exempt from CLIA
Nothing, as long as the physician is told the result is research grade
The institutional review board can grant a CLIA exemption
Releasing the result for diagnosis, prevention, or treatment brings the testing under CLIA, so it must be performed in a CLIA-certified laboratory
explanation: The research exception holds only while results are not reported for patient-specific care. Once a result is released for assessing health or diagnosing, preventing, or treating an individual, the testing falls under CLIA. A 'research grade' disclaimer does not restore the exception, because it is the use of the result that decides.

stem: A laboratory certified for chemistry and haematology wants to begin immunohematology testing. What does CLIA require?
choices: The laboratory must be certified for each specialty and subspecialty in which it performs testing
One certificate covers any test the laboratory chooses to add
A separate CLIA number is issued for each new instrument
No action, as long as the complexity matches its current testing
explanation: Laboratories must be certified for each specialty and subspecialty of testing they perform, so adding immunohematology means adding that specialty. Matching complexity is the tempting shortcut, but complexity and specialty are separate dimensions of the certificate.

stem: A CAP-accredited laboratory asks whether CLIA still applies to it. What is the answer?
choices: Yes: it holds a CLIA certificate of accreditation, an approved accreditor's requirements may be more stringent than CLIA's, and the state survey agency still enforces CLIA
No: accreditation by an approved organization replaces CLIA certification
Yes, but only for its waived testing
Only if the laboratory bills Medicare
explanation: Accreditation does not replace CLIA. The laboratory holds a CLIA certificate of accreditation, the approved accrediting organization's standards may impose more stringent requirements than CLIA itself, and state survey agencies continue to set and enforce CLIA requirements. Billing is irrelevant: CLIA follows the testing, not the payer.

stem: A reagent label carries the GHS pictogram showing a human silhouette with a white starburst on the chest. What does it flag?
choices: Acute toxicity that can be fatal in small amounts
Serious longer-term health hazards such as carcinogenicity or target organ toxicity
Skin and eye corrosion
Flammability
explanation: The health-hazard pictogram marks carcinogens, respiratory sensitizers, reproductive and target organ toxicity, and aspiration hazards. Acute toxicity that can kill in small amounts carries the skull and crossbones, corrosion has its own pictogram, and the flame marks flammables — reading the silhouette as 'poison' is the usual error.

stem: Before opening a new solvent you need to know which gloves and eye protection the manufacturer specifies. Which safety data sheet section has it?
choices: Section 2, Hazard(s) identification
Section 9, Physical and chemical properties
Section 8, Exposure controls/personal protection
The shipping label on the outer carton
explanation: Section 8 gives exposure limits, engineering controls, and the personal protective equipment for the chemical. Section 2 is tempting because it names the hazards and carries the signal word and pictograms, but it does not tell you which glove and eye protection to put on.

stem: What governs the order of sections in a safety data sheet?
choices: A standardized 16-section format in a fixed order, with first-aid measures always in Section 4
Manufacturers may order the sections as they wish, as long as the information is all present
An eight-section format set by each state
The distributor sets the order, not the manufacturer
explanation: Hazard communication requires safety data sheets in a uniform 16-section format presented in a set order, so first-aid measures are Section 4 and handling and storage Section 7 whoever made the product. The fixed order is the point: in an emergency nobody should have to search the sheet.

stem: Which set of elements must appear on the label of a hazardous chemical container shipped to the laboratory?
choices: Product identifier, lot number, expiration date, and storage temperature
Chemical name, CAS number, and the biohazard symbol
Product identifier, signal word, and the receiving department
Product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, and supplier information
explanation: Shipped-container labels carry six elements: product identifier, signal word, hazard statement(s), pictogram(s), precautionary statement(s), and the name, address, and telephone number of the responsible party. Lot number and expiration date appear on many reagent labels and are useful inventory data, but they are not hazard communication label elements.

stem: When must employees receive hazard communication training?
choices: At the annual safety in-service only
At initial assignment, and again whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into their work area
Only when a chemical changes supplier
Within 90 days of any chemical spill
explanation: Training is required at the time of initial assignment to work involving hazardous chemicals and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into the work area. An annual refresher is good practice, but waiting for it leaves staff working with an unfamiliar hazard untrained in the meantime.

stem: A stock bottle of acid has a torn label: the product name is still readable but the hazard statements and pictograms are gone. What do you do?
choices: Keep using it, because the safety data sheet on file carries the same information
Write the chemical name on the cap in marker and keep it in service
Relabel the container with the required label information before it is used again
Move it to the back of the cabinet and flag it at the annual inventory
explanation: Labels on incoming containers must not be removed or defaced, and containers must stay legibly labelled with the required information, so a damaged label is replaced before the next use. Having the safety data sheet on file is the tempting excuse, but the label is what warns the person holding the bottle at the moment they pour.

stem: How often must the written Exposure Control Plan be reviewed and updated?
choices: At least annually, and whenever new or modified tasks and procedures affect occupational exposure
Only after an exposure incident occurs
Every three years, at facility licence renewal
Whenever a new employee is hired
explanation: The plan is reviewed and updated at least annually and whenever tasks or procedures change. The update must document the employer's consideration of safer medical devices and reflect input from frontline employees who use them. Updating only after an incident is the reactive habit the annual review exists to prevent.

stem: What does the sharps injury log record?
choices: The injured employee's name, job title, and post-exposure test results
The type and brand of device involved, the department or work area where the incident occurred, and an explanation of how it happened
Only the number of injuries each quarter
The source patient's identity and diagnosis
explanation: The sharps injury log records the device type and brand, the work area, and how the injury occurred, and it is kept in a way that protects the injured employee's privacy. Names and test results belong in the confidential medical record, not in a log whose purpose is spotting patterns in devices and tasks.

stem: A phlebotomist with occupational exposure declines the hepatitis B vaccination series. What happens?
choices: The refusal is final; the employer need not offer the series again
The employee must be reassigned to duties without exposure
The employee pays for the series if they request it later
The employee signs the declination statement, and the vaccine remains available at no cost if they later change their mind while still covered
explanation: A worker who declines signs the OSHA declination statement, and the employer must still make the vaccination available later, at no cost, if the employee changes their mind while occupational exposure continues. Treating the refusal as permanent, or billing the employee afterwards, is the opposite of what the standard requires.

stem: What does the OSHA laboratory standard require of the Chemical Hygiene Plan?
choices: That it be readily available to employees, reviewed and evaluated for effectiveness at least annually and updated as necessary, with a designated Chemical Hygiene Officer
That it be kept in the director's office for inspectors
That it be rewritten whenever a new chemical is purchased
That it replace the need for safety data sheets at the bench
explanation: The Chemical Hygiene Plan must be capable of protecting employees, readily available to them, reviewed and evaluated for effectiveness at least annually and updated as necessary, and the employer must designate a Chemical Hygiene Officer. A plan filed away for inspectors fails the availability requirement that makes it useful at the bench.

stem: Who pays for the personal protective equipment required at the bench?
choices: The employee, as a condition of employment
The employer for the first set only
The employer, including replacements, except for PPE the employee has lost or intentionally damaged
The cost is split between employer and employee
explanation: Required PPE is provided at no cost to the employee, and the employer pays for replacements as well. 'First set only' is the tempting half-answer: worn, contaminated, or defective PPE is replaced at the employer's expense as often as the work requires. The single exception is equipment the employee lost or intentionally damaged.

stem: Before assigning PPE in a new work area, what must the employer do?
choices: Assess the area for hazards requiring PPE, select equipment that properly fits each affected employee, communicate the selection to them, and certify the hazard assessment in writing
Walk the area with the supervisor and order gloves on that basis
Document an assessment only once an injury has occurred
Let each employee choose the PPE they prefer
explanation: The employer assesses the workplace for hazards, selects PPE that fits each affected employee, communicates that selection, and certifies in writing that the assessment was performed — identifying the workplace evaluated, the person certifying, and the date. A verbal walk-through leaves no certification and no record of which hazards were considered.

stem: A tube slips and shatters on the bench, leaving blood-contaminated glass. How is it picked up?
choices: With gloved hands, into a red biohazard bag
With mechanical means such as a brush and dustpan, tongs, or forceps, into a sharps container, decontaminating the surface afterwards
Swept into the regular trash once the blood has dried
Rinsed into the sink and wiped down with disinfectant
explanation: Contaminated broken glassware is never picked up directly with the hands, gloved or not: it is lifted with mechanical means into a puncture-resistant container, and the surface is then decontaminated. Gloves plus a red bag is the tempting answer because the bag is the usual destination for contaminated items, but a bag is not puncture resistant and the glass will find the next pair of hands.

stem: Which pairing correctly separates an engineering control from a work-practice control?
choices: Engineering: a self-sheathing needle. Work practice: the prohibition on two-handed recapping
Engineering: the face shield worn while aliquoting. Work practice: the sharps container
Engineering: hand washing after glove removal. Work practice: the biosafety cabinet
Engineering: the Exposure Control Plan. Work practice: the sharps injury log
explanation: Engineering controls isolate or remove the hazard from the workplace — self-sheathing needles, sharps containers, biosafety cabinets. Work-practice controls change how the task is performed, such as banning two-handed recapping in favour of a one-handed scoop. A face shield is neither: PPE is its own category, worn on the body because the hazard could not be removed.

stem: You pick up the face shield before an aliquoting run and find the visor cracked across the eye line. What do you do?
choices: Take it out of service and fetch an undamaged replacement before starting
Use it for this short run and report it at the end of the shift
Tape the crack on the inside and carry on
Wear safety glasses underneath the cracked shield
explanation: Defective or damaged personal protective equipment must not be used: it comes out of service and is replaced, at the employer's expense. 'Just this once, it is a short run' is exactly the reasoning the rule blocks, because a cracked visor can fail at the splash it was meant to stop.

stem: You have finished processing specimens and need to document the run at the office computer. What is correct?
choices: Remove and discard the contaminated gloves in the designated container before leaving the work area, then wash your hands
Keep the gloves on so bare hands never touch the keyboard
Wash the gloved hands at the sink and keep wearing them
Remove the gloves at the office and drop them in the office bin
explanation: Gloves are removed and discarded in the designated container before leaving the work area, and hands are washed immediately afterwards. Keeping them on feels protective, which is the trap: contamination then travels to door handles, keyboards, and phones that nobody treats as dirty.

stem: Which statement describes how specimens are handled under standard precautions in the clinical laboratory?
choices: Extra precautions are used only for specimens flagged as infectious
Every patient specimen is handled as potentially infectious, whatever test was requested or diagnosis is known
Precautions depend on the ward the specimen came from
Barrier protection is needed only for specimens from known positive patients
explanation: Clinical laboratories work at Biosafety Level 2 practices and treat all human blood, body fluids, and tissues as potentially infectious, because the specimen that transmits infection is usually the one nobody suspected. Relying on flags means relying on a diagnosis that has not been made yet.

stem: Which practice preserves the containment of a Class II biological safety cabinet during use?
choices: Stacking racks and supplies along the front grille to free working space
Working close to the sash opening so the downflow does not disturb the work
Working well inside the cabinet, moving the arms slowly straight in and out, and keeping the front grille unobstructed
Raising the sash above the marked working height for easier access
explanation: Class II protection depends on a stable air curtain at the opening: work is done well inside the cabinet, arms move slowly and straight in and out, and the grilles stay clear. Blocking the front grille with racks or absorbent paper interrupts the inflow that keeps aerosols away from the operator — the most common way a cabinet is defeated while still appearing to work.

stem: A mercury thermometer breaks on the floor by the chemistry bench and beads scatter across the tile. Which action is prohibited?
choices: Vacuuming or sweeping the beads, or washing them down the drain
Keeping people out of the area and reporting the spill
Ventilating the area to the outside
Collecting the beads onto a damp paper towel in a sealed bag
explanation: Never vacuum a mercury spill: a vacuum throws mercury vapour into the room air. Never sweep it either, because a broom breaks the beads into smaller droplets that spread further, and never pour mercury down a drain, where it lodges in the plumbing. Keep people out, ventilate to the outside, and use the mercury spill procedure.

stem: During cleanup of a broken mercury thermometer, how are the beads collected and the area handled afterwards?
choices: Roll the beads together with stiff cardboard or draw them up with an eyedropper onto a damp paper towel, seal them in a labelled bag, and ventilate the area to the outside for at least 24 hours
Rinse the residue into the sink with detergent and dry the floor
Absorb the beads with kitty litter and discard it in the regular trash
Wipe the beads up with alcohol gauze and discard it in the biohazard bag
explanation: Beads are rolled together with stiff cardboard or lifted with an eyedropper onto a damp paper towel, sealed in a labelled bag, and the area is kept ventilated to the outside for at least 24 hours; the local health department or waste authority directs disposal. Absorbent litter is the tempting habit from solvent spills, but it does not take up metallic mercury, and rinsing it down the drain contaminates the plumbing.

stem: A new analyzer needs power and the nearest outlet is already in use. Which practice is acceptable?
choices: Daisy-chain a second power strip into the first to reach the instrument
Tape over the cracked insulation on the existing cord and share the outlet
Run an extension cord along the floor as the permanent supply
Power the instrument from permanent wiring, inspecting cords before use and removing damaged ones from service
explanation: Cord- and plug-connected equipment is visually inspected before use on each shift and taken out of service when damage is found; extension cords and chained power strips are temporary measures, never a substitute for permanent wiring. Taping damaged insulation hides the defect instead of removing the equipment from service.

stem: A routine diagnostic specimen is shipped to a reference laboratory as a Category B infectious substance. How is the outer package marked?
choices: A biohazard label on the outer box is sufficient
With the UN 3373 diamond mark and the words 'Biological Substance, Category B' next to it
A red 'Infectious' sticker plus the sender's return address
No marking is needed when the shipment travels by courier
explanation: Category B shipments carry the UN 3373 diamond-shaped mark on the outer package with the proper shipping name 'Biological Substance, Category B' adjacent to it, on top of triple packaging. A generic biohazard label is tempting because it is the familiar in-house symbol, but it tells the carrier neither the classification nor how to respond to damage in transit.

stem: Where must emergency eyewash and drenching facilities be located in a laboratory working with corrosives?
choices: Within the work area, suitable for immediate emergency use wherever eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials
In the facility's first-aid room, which all staff are shown during orientation
Anywhere in the building, as long as the route is signposted
At the nearest restroom sink
explanation: Where the eyes or body of any person may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing must be provided within the work area for immediate emergency use. A first-aid room down the hall fails that test: a corrosive in the eye has to be flushed within seconds, not after a walk.

stem: Water is spreading across the floor from a leaking pipe under the laboratory sink. What is the correct response?
choices: Mop it up and carry on, since the leak is small
Tighten the fitting yourself to stop the leak
Keep staff off the wet floor, guard or mark the area, and report the leak so it is corrected before the surface is used again
Leave it for the next shift with a note on the bench
explanation: Walking-working surfaces are kept clean and, so far as feasible, dry and free of hazards such as leaks and spills; a hazardous condition must be corrected or repaired before the surface is used again, and guarded in the meantime. Mopping is tempting because it makes the floor look fine while the leak keeps running, and the repair itself belongs to qualified people, not to whoever found the puddle.

stem: The sharps container at the draw station has filled to the fill line. What is correct?
choices: Close it and put a fresh container in service; sharps containers are puncture resistant, leakproof, labelled or colour-coded, and closable
Press the contents down to make room until the end of the shift
Transfer the contents into a second container
Take the lid off so the last few sharps will fit
explanation: Sharps containers are puncture resistant, leakproof on sides and bottom, labelled or colour-coded, and closable, and they are replaced before they overfill. Pressing the contents down or reaching in to transfer them puts a hand into a container full of contaminated needles — the exact injury the container exists to prevent.

stem: Where does spent xylene from the staining line go?
choices: Down the sink with plenty of running water
Into the red biohazard bag
Into a labelled, compatible hazardous chemical waste container, handled under the Chemical Hygiene Plan
Into the autoclave with the day's infectious waste
explanation: Spent solvent is hazardous chemical waste: it goes into a labelled container compatible with the solvent, under the disposal provisions of the laboratory's Chemical Hygiene Plan. Flushing it away with water is the tempting shortcut and discharges a flammable regulated solvent into the sewer; neither a red bag nor the autoclave is a route for chemical waste.
